paragraphs.heading: A metal mixed with something else
paragraphs.text: An alloy is a mixture of two or more elements, at least one of them a metal, that keeps the character of a metal. The main metal is called the base or primary metal, and the alloy may share its name. Inside an alloy the atoms are joined by metallic bonding, not by the covalent bonds typical of chemical compounds.

paragraphs.heading: Why metals get alloyed
paragraphs.text: An alloy often behaves differently from the pure elements it is made from. Most metals used commercially are alloyed to make them better, for example stronger, harder or more resistant to corrosion. Alloying can also lower cost, as with gold mixed with copper. The results are everywhere: steel in buildings, cars and surgical tools, titanium alloys in aerospace, and beryllium-copper for tools that do not spark.

paragraphs.heading: Small additions, big changes
paragraphs.text: Aluminium and copper are both very soft and ductile, yet an alloy of the two is much stronger. Adding a little carbon to iron swaps iron's great ductility for the extra strength of steel. Adding chromium to steel makes stainless steel, which resists corrosion better, while adding silicon changes its electrical behaviour to make silicon steel.

paragraphs.heading: Limits to mixing
paragraphs.text: Like oil and water, a molten metal does not always mix with another element. Lithium, magnesium and silver, for instance, barely dissolve in pure iron at all. Even when two ingredients do dissolve, there is usually a saturation point beyond which no more can be added. Iron can stably hold at most 6.67% carbon, which forms a compound called cementite.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the crystals
paragraphs.text: If the metals stay dissolved as they solidify, the alloy becomes a solid solution: one uniform structure of identical crystals, called a phase. If they stop dissolving as the mix cools, they can separate into two or more kinds of crystal, some richer in one ingredient than another. When some alloys are cooled very fast, they first form a single phase overloaded with the added elements. Over time those atoms move out of the crystal lattice and form a second phase that strengthens the crystals from within.

paragraphs.heading: Old and new alloys
paragraphs.text: Some alloys occur naturally, such as electrum, a mix of silver and gold. Bronze, made of tin and copper, was one of the first alloys people made, and it is much stronger and harder than either metal. In ancient times steel could only be made by accident, as a byproduct of heating iron ore in fires to make iron. Most alloys, including various aluminium, titanium, nickel and magnesium alloys, were not created until the 1900s.
